title: The Wicker Filmmakers Break Down The Sex Scenes Between Olivia Colman And Alexander Skarsgård
text:
The Wicker Filmmakers Break Down The Sex Scenes Between Olivia Colman And Alexander Skarsgård

Wicker season is almost here. And no, we don’t mean it’s time to stock up on baskets, chairs or furniture… we mean it’s time for the horny, romantic and bitingly funny film Wicker, starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård, to take over our lives. You may have seen countless memes online about women thirsting over the Wicker Husband, played by Skarsgård, and described as “fuckable furniture” by another character, but rest assured: this film isn’t just a quick wicker romp. It’s a commentary on society — how single women are treated, what happens when you uphold the patriarchy, and what it means to truly fall in love. Oh, and it will leave you swooning.

It follows Colman’s Fisherwoman, an outcast in a medieval farming town due to her fishy smell and spinster status. When the community’s jeers become too much to bear, she decides to commission herself a wicker husband. What ensues is absolute chaos. For the Fisherwoman, it’s the first time she experiences unconditional love. For the villagers, it’s the first time seeing a man not abide by the patriarchy, which causes absolute chaos.

When I spoke with the husband-and-wife team behind Wicker, writers and directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, they said filming the intimate scenes was a highlight, but they also appreciate how audiences seem to connect with the film on a deeper level.

Refinery29 Australia: How did you get Olivia Colman on board? I imagine explaining she has to get intimate with a man made out of wicker would be a bit awkward.

Eleanor Wilson: Yeah. It’s funny, when we first spoke to her about that, it was sort of like, “Don’t worry, the sex scenes are just going to be funny. It’s just going to be played for laughs.” But it was surprisingly sexier than we thought it was going to be.

Alex Huston Fischer: She would have never signed up for it.

EW: Had she known.

While the film is hilarious and there’s some really strange smut scenes, it’s also wholesome. Do you think people will find it more romantic and sweet than they anticipated?

EW: That’s what we’re finding, actually. When we made the trailer, obviously you want to put lots of fun things in there to make people want to see the movie. We feel assured that there’s so much more to the movie than what’s depicted in the trailer. There’s a lot more story, and there’s a lot more heart.

AHF: We even surprised ourselves when we were writing it that it just turned into a sweeping romance. The film is a couple of things, but that’s one of them for sure. It’s pretty romantic, and we made each other cry sometimes while writing it.

EW: It is essentially a film about relationships. But I think when we got into writing The Fisherwoman and what’s going on for her, it was quite personal, and we did put a lot of ourselves in it. I think writing from that place can ultimately be quite moving.

AHF: And we had been writing our own vows around the same time. We got married a couple of months before we started writing the movie. So we were like thinking about our own vows, and then we were writing this. So it all leaked into this.

Did you expect there would be so many women going wild for the Wicker Husband?

EW: No!

AHF: Not this crazy. We weren’t expecting the internet explosion, but we did know that he was stunning, and we were excited to show everyone what he looked like.

EW: I think one of the interesting things about the reaction, though, is that it’s not just that he’s very visually spectacular, but I think people are picking up on the fact that he does things without being asked, and that he doesn’t require a pat on the back for every task that he does, and there’s something about that aspect of the Wicker Husband, I think, that is even maybe the sexiest thing about him.

AHF: Proactively helpful. There’s nothing hotter than that.

It’s not all about “fuckable furniture”, though. The themes of patriarchy feel really relevant today, even though we’re so far from the time it’s set in.

EW: Especially with Elizabeth Debicki’s character. We were really talking a lot about that with her and the position that her character’s in, and how that sort of informs all her choices throughout the film. You know, it’s just intrinsically there.

AHF: It’s vaguely 17th century. We invented the time and place, but it’s all the same stuff we’re talking about now, and it’s sadly very relevant.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

But of course, people will be talking about the sex scenes. What was it like to film? He’s in a practical suit.

EW: Intimate scenes on films in general actually sometimes end up being the most fun because, because you do a closed set, there’s very few people in the room, and it feels like you’re just making a short film with your friends again. So it was really just the two of them: our wonderful intimacy coordinator Ita O’Brien, Lol Crawley, who shot it, us and sound, and that’s it. It’s a small environment. No one’s even watching monitors in these scenes, so you’re kind of doing this secret little thing in your own little hut.

AHF: It’s kind of like stunt choreography. You’re just coming up with what feels right and what makes sense. And we all had ideas, and it was kind of a fun brainstorm.

EW: The fun thing about the suit as well was once you add that element to it, things change too. There’s a moment where Olivia’s fingers sort of slip into the weave of his back, which we didn’t write. It’s such a beautiful moment, and that’s something that could only have come out of the practical suit being there.

Do you think there’s going to be any cosplay, for Halloween or in the bedroom?

EW: I hope so!

AHF: Well, we did have a screening in L.A. at Beyond Fest the other night, and some women dressed up as the Fisherwoman. We invite it, and it seems like a lot of fun.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Wicker is in theaters now.

title: The Gilded Age’s George & Bertha Russell Are TV’s Best Couple. Carrie Coon & Morgan Spector Tell Us Why
text:
The Gilded Age’s George & Bertha Russell Are TV’s Best Couple. Carrie Coon & Morgan Spector Tell Us Why

George and Bertha Russell’s marriage is in trouble. In Season 4 of The Gilded Age, the once-unbreakable power couple of New York’s elite are at odds — they’re also an ocean apart. In the season premiere, which aired last night, Bertha (Carrie Coon) is in England with the daughter she married off to a duke after much scheming and plotting as she gives birth to their grandson. While railroad tycoon George (Morgan Spector) is unraveling under the pressure of maintaining an empire and the impending doom of pesky anti-monopoly laws. Last season, he moved out of their house. This season, he’s barely tolerating his wife. It’s a far cry from the doting, sexy, us-against-the-world energy the Russells were giving in Season 1. But the chill between their characters is the exact opposite vibe Coon and Spector exude in real life. 

Together, the actors are warm and playful, complimenting each other frequently and passionately defending their political outspokenness. They sit shoulder to shoulder across from me at the Plaza Hotel in New York City and slip easily from joking about Spector taking up the mantle of Sexiest Man Alive from reigning SMA title holder Noah Wyle to raging about how the arts are under attack and the ills of capitalism. It’s that duality — from silly to serious — that makes The Gilded Age so great. It’s a show about how America has systemically enfranchised its workers and how the uber rich got richer, and it’s a show about the feigned importance of the placement of a salad fork and the etiquette of party invites. It’s about race and class, and it’s about the scandal of premarital sex in the 1900s. It’s about politics and parties. It’s a calming, simple watch with low stakes about frivolous ambition and romance and it’s a commentary on America, racism, gender roles, and the complexity of marriage. 

It’s the latter where Coon and Spector shine. And in our conversation, they make it clear that they are very aware of the chokehold their characters have on the internet. After a slow burn for the series (it barely survived Season 1 but HBO let it cook), the series has now reached peak interest and both actors are the subject of thirst edits and obsessive fan fixation. For those of us who have been riding for the Russells since day one, we welcome the new members to the Railroad Daddy and Opera Mommy hive. I promise those nicknames are earned. Coon and Spector aren’t just ridiculously attractive (obviously), they bring gravitas and glamor to the couple while also lacing the characters with grit, magnetism, and voracity that makes watching them addictive. Here, the pair break down why their characters have struck a chord with audiences, the authenticity of their political statements, and why Coon says Season 4 is “Morgan’s season.” 

I love my parents, George and Bertha Russell! We saw these characters as such a unit for the first season, then last season they were breaking apart, and now they are still at odds. You obviously have a great rapport. Is it fun to play mad at each other or do you miss the unity? 

Carrie Coon: Awww. 

Morgan Spector: Both.  I actually found it so refreshing to be portraying a marriage that really worked, especially in this period.

CC: We were sad in Season 3.  We were fighting a lot in Season 3. 

MS:  Yeah, we were fighting a lot in Season 3. And this season we’re on islands. We’re alienated from each other, and we’re struggling to even communicate at all.  It was delicate charting our routes back to each other this season. That was pretty collaborative so that was fun and interesting and exciting to try to figure out  how do they find their way back to each other?  Why do they do it and what are the moments where they really start to re-solidify as a couple? 

CC:  And in the midst of that, Morgan had this incredible acting challenge of having to figure out charting this addiction story as well.  To me, it’s Morgan’s season in a way that I love. In a way that I’m totally behind. 

MS:  [whispers] You haven’t seen it though. 

CC: I haven’t seen it, no.  But I feel like what was asked of you was the stuff actors dream of. You really rose to the occasion. There was a lot of delight in watching you take that on in a way that we didn’t have in Season 3 of just being in the outs. But this was being able to sit back and admire how you were charting it [and] being proud of you. 

 I love this relationship between the two of you and how much admiration there is. 

CC: It’s real.

It is really beautiful as a fan to see. Last time we talked, you went a little viral for your thoughts on billionaires.

MS: Oh, yeah. 

CC: Oopsies! 

Why has it been important for both of you to speak out about class and be critical of capitalism even though or because you’re playing these characters?

CC:  I don’t know that it’s confined to our publicity for this show. I think Morgan and I have always been politically engaged.  A lot of the actors on this show are. It’s something we respect about each other. We’re theater people. There’s been a war on the arts forever. We are fundamentally hoping for more access to all of the arts and services. Our people are very vulnerable people in the world right now. And so I find that what actually indemnifies you against criticism in some ways is authenticity. The people on this show have kind of always been engaged in that conversation. They’re not suddenly getting involved in it. And I feel like that protects us sometimes from some of the blowback people get when they jump into politics because they have a show that’s suddenly speaking to a moment.

MS: Right. 

CC: And I just feel like we haven’t necessarily been moving through the world that way. Is that true? 

MS:  I think that’s true. A lot of people on our show are politically aware and politically active, outspoken people prior to this show and they will be after the show., I think it is definitely true that for this show, we end up talking about politics during press for this show because the parallels between then and now are so direct and stark.  So it’s impossible not to. Having a group of very politically conscious people who are having to talk about this subject matter, you’re inevitably gonna get commentary  on the present day because it’s just there. 

CC: It’s just the truth.  

When you are watching the show, there are these stark parallels to the present day. George is fighting against monopoly laws this season, which of course has real-word parallels. Is it frustrating or is it hopeful to know these issues have been going on for so long? 

MS: I think it’s really interesting because the rapid urbanization, rapid industrialization, the hyper-concentration of wealth in a small minority. The monopoly capitalism, et cetera, all of that led to massive reforms, right? It led to trust busting. It led to the New Deal in some ways. And it led to huge reorganizations of American society in really fundamental ways. And then we basically forgot all of the lessons of this era. And I think that was basically, you know, there were many factors: globalization, like the sort of offshoring of labor. I mean, we’ve really separated the factory floor and capital, and even the American consumer. Those things all used to be kind of in the same place, and now they’re far-flung all over the globe, often in many different places. And so organizing against the power of concentrated capital doesn’t work the same way it used to. It used to be, you’d have people on the factory floor of a particular factory. In Season 2 — Season Two is our union season, right?

CC: Yeah. [laughs] 

MS: It was — yeah. So, you know, when those guys wanted to shut down your factory, they actually had a tremendous amount of leverage over you. Now, if somebody wants to change, let’s say, Apple’s practices, it’s a factory in Shenzhen or something like that that’s going to have to actually exert that kind of leverage in order to affect an American company. It’s a very different world, but in a lot of ways, I think the results that we’re seeing from the same concentration of wealth, the same concentration of power, are really similar, especially in terms of democracy. Because you cannot have so much power and so much wealth concentrated in so few hands, especially in a political system like ours that is so porous when it comes to money, when it comes to political money, without seeing real destruction of democracy, and I think that’s what we’re seeing. I think our government does not work for ordinary people.

CC: It’s not working for anybody right now.

MS: I think that’s just sort of objectively true, right? There’s a very famous Princeton study showing the preferences of the actual voter versus the preferences of the donors, and the donors get what they want every single time, and the voter gets what they want zero times.

They’re not beholden to us at all. We have really lost control of this apparatus. I think looking to the 19th century, looking to what people did in order to take back some power in similar circumstances is instructive and should be for all of us.

CC:  As a woman, yes, it’s very frustrating. 

MS: [laughs]

CS: Here, here. 

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 (@refinery29)

 This is why we love both of you. This was also the energy you brought to the billionaire conversation. Carrie, I love how straightforward you are. Let’s take a hard pivot to talk about Railroad Daddy. Now, he’s Railroad Granddaddy. 

MS: Hell yeah. 

CC: Still sexy. 

 How much do you love or hate that nickname and the thirst that happens surrounding the character? 

MS:  What’s to hate? Look, to be sexually objectified as a straight man – a straight white man — is honestly a gift. It’s rare. 

CC:  Move over, [Sexiest Man Alive] Noah Wyle. Next year, Morgan Spector’s coming for you. 

MS:  It’s nice. Train Daddy is another [nickname] and this year, I’m trying to get Trainspotting Daddy started. You know what I mean? Because of the drug addiction going on. Trying to get that started. 

CC: Yeah,  we gotta get that out there. 

MS:  it’s funny. It’s lovely, and I do think it’s the character more than it is me. But it’s nice. What, what can I say? 

Carrie and I are both like, “no, it’s not.” 

CC:  We’re like, “No.” No, no. But keep telling yourself. That’s part of your charm. 

Bertha’s also got stans too! What is it about her that people love so much?

CC: She’s a gay icon! 

MS: [laughs] She’s a gay icon! 

CC:  What’s not to love? Fabulous dresses. So much swagger. It’s the walk.  She’s the ultimate diva. She gets what she wants. She fights for what she wants. She cuts through the BS. She’ll play by the rules until the rules are not serving her, and then she’ll be like, “I see that rule, and I think it’s BS.” And I love that about her. But she also fights really hard for the people she loves, so she has integrity, too. You may not always agree with the way she gets somewhere, but she really is ruthless for her people, and I think that’s a really important quality. And because George and Bertha are fundamentally outsiders and disruptors, we have wealth and power, but we are actually trying to get in, and that is about belonging. Bertha’s fighting to belong, and that’s such an American thing. That’s the spirit of what it meant to come here. We were escaping one sort of tyrannical regime to kind of build a new world, and everyone’s kind of fighting their way in to  have influence and power, and Bertha and George are doing that. And also, her amazing dresses.

MS: She’s fabulous. 

CC:  I mean, she just looks fly. Does anybody say that anymore?  I feel like that was a ’90s holdover and I was like in In Living Color all of a sudden. 

MS: We’re children of the ’90s so we’re allowed. We can keep saying it. 

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

title: Trump Wants You to Believe Non-Citizens Can Vote. They Can’t (But They’re Counting on You To)
text:
Trump Wants You to Believe Non-Citizens Can Vote. They Can’t (But They’re Counting on You To)

Throughout President Donald Trump’s latest term in office, he has alleged that undocumented immigrants vote en masse in U.S. elections, framing the group, which can’t legally vote in federal or state elections, as the key culprits behind a widespread voting fraud scheme in the country. The truth: While this myth persists, the numbers show that election fraud, in general, is very rare. According to a report from The Brennan Center, reported cases of voter fraud amount to less than 1%. And the number of non-citizens who vote illegally is even smaller.

I would know. I became a green card holder in the spring of 2026, which means I still have years to wait before I can take the final steps toward U.S. citizenship and begin voting.  

Since 1996, federal law has made it illegal for non-citizens to vote in federal elections, including presidential and congressional races for the U.S. House and Senate. Knowingly voting in a federal election as a non-citizen can carry criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and serious immigration consequences, including deportation. Even more, knowingly and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to register to vote or cast a ballot in any federal, state, or local election is a federal crime punishable by up to five years in prison.

But that hasn’t stopped Trump, or the Republican party more broadly, from spreading false narratives about immigrants, especially Latine immigrants, and elections. 

“This is part of a wider strategy we’ve been seeing in the past two years, by instilling fear, intimidation, and attacking our democracy,” Carmen M. Feliciano, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy at UnidosUS, tells Refinery29 Somos. 

In asserting these election myths, Trump and his party not only spread misinformation about Latine immigrants, but they also make his supporters suspicious of Latines altogether, questioning the status and legality of Latine citizens waiting to cast their ballot on Election Day.

“The reality is out of 10 Latinos right now in the United States, eight are U.S. citizens. … Every 30 seconds, a Latino citizen turns 18 and becomes eligible to vote,” Feliciano says. “We are a growing population. We are a force to reckon with. … We know that our community can change the election results if we go out to vote and exercise our constitutional right to vote.”

But this requires those in our community with U.S. citizenship to hit the polls. About 50.6% of eligible Latine voters actually voted in the 2024 Presidential Election. And while that percentage is higher than in past races, it still fares lower than other racial or ethnic groups. In fact, eligible non-Latine white voters have a turnout rate of 70.5%, non-Latine Black voters have a turnout rate of 59.6%, and Asian-Americans a turnout rate of 57.1%.

Voting is an act of labor and should be a symbol of commitment to a community we care for. 

Why Non-Citizens Need Citizens to Vote

I can’t vote yet, but if you can, do it — we need you to. 

Since returning to office, the Trump administration has dramatically expanded its efforts to target, harass, detain, and deport immigrants. It has ramped up Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and arrests in communities across the country, expanded fast-track deportations that can bypass immigration court hearings, increased immigration detention, and moved to strip temporary protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants. It has also targeted asylum access and even birthright citizenship. The result is an increasingly hostile and uncertain environment for immigrants, not just those without legal status, but also people with temporary protections, legal residency, and families with mixed immigration statuses.

And it’s not just immigration policies. Like U.S. citizens, non-citizens are navigating an increasingly expensive cost of living, worrying about everything from groceries and rent to healthcare and the cost of raising children.

One issue I’m especially concerned about is the potential substantial changes coming in the 2030 census, like Trump’s plan to remove race and ethnicity questions and data. This is dangerous. Latine nonprofits, grassroots organizations, and even Hispanic-Serving-Institutions (HSIs) in higher education cannot function or sustain without grant-funded programs or community-based financial support. A census undercount for Latines can mean fewer resources for schools, clinics, and local infrastructure, which affects citizens and non-citizens alike. 

Last month, I wrapped up my role as a program assistant at an HSI that serves mostly Latine and Black American students. As of September 30, that institution, Saint Peter’s University, one of the most relevant HSIs in the Latine-dense area of Jersey City, New Jersey, closed down the wellness and educational initiatives of the Bienestar For All program, a $3 million federal Title V grant-funded project from the  U.S. Department of Education – a devastating loss for my team and our students, most of whom are food insecure and lack the adequate wellness education they need to succeed in college. 

“Our younger generation needs to understand that voting is necessary to express our opinions. It is a sacred right at the base of our democracy,” Feliciano says.

So when you hit the polls for the midterms, remember those of us who can’t, those who are disenfranchised even while we’re being disparaged. When you vote, take your family, your friends, and your neighbors. Make a day out of it. Bring snacks, bring music, and make the trip something people look forward to rather than something they dread. There will be lines, and that’s okay. Wait through them. If you’re worried about making it before the polling place closes, don’t let that discourage you. In most states, if you’re already standing in line when the polls close, you still get to cast your ballot. 

And when the day is over, keep going. Follow trusted pages and publications that cover these issues, ideally bilingual ones, so that nobody in your household gets left out of the conversation. Learn how local, state, and federal politics work and get involved beyond voting. 

“Know who your member of Congress is, who is your senator. How do they represent you? Go to a town hall meeting. Ask questions. Every member of Congress has a district office. They’re not in D.C. all the time. Every week members of Congress go back to their district office, and as a constituent, you have the right to go to their offices and ask questions. They owe you a response,” Feliciano adds.

Be responsible with your political conscience, because it’s one of the most powerful things you have. 

How Non-Citizens Can Show Up Even Though We Can’t Vote

While non-citizen Latines can’t vote, there are other ways we can show up. Beyond the ballot, green card or visa holders, just like any other immigrant with any kind of official documentation, can still take part in civic life. They can volunteer, organize, attend public meetings, speak at town halls, protest, and support civic engagement groups, especially those with a grassroots structure. 

Johanna Toruño, artist and founder of the public art project The Unapologetic Street Series, does not let her immigration status stop her from civic engagement. “As a person who can’t vote in this country yet, I’ve found ways to feel involved because it can feel quite daunting to not be able to participate in the decision-making,” the El Salvador-born, Los Angeles-based artist tells Somos. “I canvass, volunteer my time to campaigns I believe in, and organize with neighbors and friends to push voters to do exactly that — engage.” 

Toruño also gets real with her community about the ways misinformation and religious conservatism impacts the ways in which they vote. “Latines tend to be more conservative and vote against their interests, and even their own values at times, because political appearances matter more,” she shares with Somos. 

She points out that religious conservatism, for instance, which is prevalent across Latin America and the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, doesn’t translate the same way in U.S. politics because “the privileges some Latines have in their home countries to allow them to be so conservative don’t apply here in the same way, but still they vote as such.” 

As a Brazilian, I saw this recently amid those living in the U.S. who cast their ballot in our homeland’s most-recent presidential election, with 62.7% of Brazilian immigrants preferring Evangelical right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro over his leftist counterpart, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. 

“I’d like Latines to explore those themes in their voting practices, especially because so many of us come from mixed-status families who pay the consequences for it, even if they agree,” Toruño adds.

Like Toruño, while I can’t vote in this year’s elections, as a green card holder, I have options to show up and forge my political voice in the best and most formative ways I can. For instance, as an adjunct lecturer in the New York City metropolitan area, I have been adapting my school curriculum and giving extra time to go over the rights and impacts of voting in class with my college students, especially since the majority of them are Latine as well. 

A passive citizen is a person who’s depriving themselves of a future with better and brighter possibilities. But political apathy can show up for those of us who are on a temporary hold, too. Our status can’t be the source of stagnant behavior. I understand it is my responsibility to be informed and to cultivate a sense of belonging with what I can learn from local, state, and national politics, even as an immigrant. Latine immigrants like Toruño are an example of how we can maximize our resources to build a sustainable future with informed and curated knowledge around politics, community care, and social justice values.

I’m showing up how I can. I’m still waiting for my turn to vote, but when it comes, when I become a U.S. citizen, I’ll show up the way I’m asking you to show up now. Because we matter. We always have, and we always will.

At the same time, in Haiti and across its diaspora, Fèt Gede honors the Gede, the spirits of death in Haitian Vodou. They’re known for their dark humor, their unapologetic sexuality, and their power to heal. Neither tradition treats death as something to fear. Both treat it as part of life, a doorway, and a reason to celebrate.

This month, we are also deep in Scorpio season, ruled by the very things most people avoid talking about: death, desire, and transformation. Scorpio knows that nothing is reborn without first being let go, and that pleasure and power live in the places we’ve been taught to hide. The New Moon in Scorpio on November 9 plants the seed of who you’re becoming. Meanwhile, on November 13, Venus and Mercury both station direct, ending the review of your love life and your truth that began in October. What you learned in the dark is now ready to be lived.

Death, sex, and rebirth aren’t taboo. They’re sacred themes that help us embrace more life. Something in your life is ending. Something in you is craving more. And someone new is emerging from what you’re finally ready to release. You can’t fully live until you’re willing to let something die.

title: Your Horoscope This Week: November 1 To 7
text:
Your Horoscope This Week: November 1 To 7

R29 babes, November begins with a much-needed cosmic breather. With no major planetary shifts this week, we have room to recalibrate while Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra continue encouraging us to review our relationships, finances, and emotional patterns. The Scorpio New Moon arrives November 9th, so consider this week your chance to get grounded before the momentum picks up. We start with the Moon in Leo joining forces with Mars and Jupiter, boosting our confidence and reminding us to align our actions with our bigger vision. Less talking about it, more being about it. 

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo for two and a half days, helping us get down to the nitty-gritty of what needs to be handled. This is the perfect time to tackle your to-do list, organize your budget, clean up your environment, or address the responsibilities that have been piling up while you’ve been busy processing life’s bigger questions. Sure, it may not be the sexiest cosmic energy, but sometimes paying that overdue bill or finally sending that email can feel just as satisfying as a major breakthrough. The trick is to avoid filling your schedule with busywork just so you can feel productive. Ask yourself which tasks will genuinely move the needle toward the goals you’re setting for November, and give those your attention first. 

Then, from November 5th through much of the 7th, the moon moves through Libra, bringing out our more social, flirtatious, and pleasure-seeking sides. After a few days of Virgo-inspired productivity, you may feel ready to dress up, spend time with friends, go on a date, browse your favorite shops, or simply surround yourself with beautiful things. With Venus retrograde in Libra, you might even find yourself rediscovering pleasures, places, or connections that once made you feel especially good. Just be mindful of impulsive spending or romantic decisions you haven’t fully thought through. This week is a reminder that even during Scorpio and retrograde season we’re allowed to lighten up and enjoy being alive. Follow the moon’s rhythm this week: dream boldly, handle your business, and give yourself something to smile about. 

Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, November begins with the Last Quarter Moon in Leo activating your romance, fame, and inner-child healing zone. A week after the Taurus Full Moon brought revelations about your money and self-worth, you may be realizing that certain pleasures, passions, or relationships deserve more of your energy, while others have become expensive distractions. Leo energy encourages you to take pride in your talents and remember what makes you feel alive. If you’ve been waiting for external validation before pursuing something you love, this lunation could help you release that hesitation. Your happiness deserves to be part of your game plan, too. 

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, bringing your attention to work, wellness, and the little habits that keep your life running smoothly. You may feel motivated to get organized, catch up on appointments, or make your schedule more manageable. Then, as the moon enters Libra on the 5th, your relationships take center stage. With Venus retrograde still unfolding in this part of your chart, a conversation with a partner or close friend could help you understand where more balance is needed. Handle your  responsibilities early in the week so you can actually enjoy connecting with people this weekend. 

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, the Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st draws your attention toward  home and the emotional foundation you’re building for yourself. After last week’s Full  Moon in your sign brought certain personal revelations to the surface, you may feel ready to make changes in your private life that reflect how much you’ve grown. Perhaps your living space needs a refresh, a family dynamic needs healthier boundaries, or you’ve simply outgrown the expectation that you should always be available to everyone. Leo energy encourages you to take ownership of your happiness. You deserve a space where you can fully be yourself, without feeling like you’re constantly performing for others. 

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon lights up your romance, creativity, and pleasure zone, making the middle of the week ideal for enjoying the little things that make life sweet. You could feel inspired to revisit a creative hobby, plan a date, or spend quality time with your children or loved ones. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your focus toward wellness and daily routines. Since your ruling planet Venus is still retrograde in Libra, pay attention to which habits genuinely make your life easier and  which ones you’ve maintained out of obligation. A little more balance in your schedule could make your weekend feel surprisingly restorative. 

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, November kicks off with the Last Quarter Moon in Leo activating your communication zone and immediate environment. A week after the Taurus Full Moon illuminated your subconscious and brought hidden emotions to the surface, you may finally be ready to put some of those revelations into words. Perhaps there’s a conversation you’ve been rehearsing in your head, an idea you’ve been sitting on, or a belief about yourself that you’re ready to challenge. Leo energy encourages you to speak with confidence, while the waning moon helps you release the need to explain yourself to everyone. Sometimes saying less, but meaning every word, is the real power move. 

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, bringing your attention toward home, family, and getting your personal environment in order. You may feel like decluttering, handling household responsibilities, or spending more time in your own company. But by the 5th, the Libra Moon activates your romance, creativity, and pleasure zone, and suddenly staying home folding laundry may sound a lot less appealing. With Venus retrograde here, an old crush, creative passion, or favorite pastime could catch your attention again. Enjoy the nostalgia without feeling pressured to recreate the past. This weekend is about remembering what makes you happy and giving yourself permission to have a little fun.

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, November begins with you being ready to secure the bag, but the Last Quarter  Moon in Leo on the 1st may have you reconsidering what you’re spending it on. After last week’s Taurus Full Moon brought revelations about your friendships, community, and future goals, you may be realizing that some of your financial priorities need to shift. Perhaps you’ve been investing too much money into keeping up socially, or you’re ready to put more resources toward a dream that actually excites you. Leo energy encourages you to recognize your talents and stop undervaluing what you bring to the table. This is a great time to release spending habits or scarcity mindsets that  have been holding you back. 

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, activating your communication zone. You may feel inspired to catch up on emails, organize your thoughts, or finally have a conversation you’ve been putting off. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your attention toward home, family, and your emotional well-being. With Venus still retrograde in Libra, you may feel more nostalgic than usual or find yourself revisiting a family matter that needs some tenderness. Keep your weekend plans flexible, Cancer. A cozy evening at home, a home-cooked meal, or quality time with people who make you feel safe could be exactly what you need. 

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, are you ready to stop carrying around a version of yourself that you’ve already outgrown? The Last Quarter Moon in your sign on November 1st encourages you to release outdated expectations about who you should be and how others perceive you. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought a professional milestone or a realization about your career direction, and now you’re being asked to consider how that evolution is changing you personally. Perhaps you’ve been putting pressure on yourself to maintain a certain image, even when it no longer feels authentic. Give yourself permission to change your mind, your appearance, or your priorities. You don’t owe anyone a permanent version of yourself. 

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon turns your attention toward money, security, and self-worth, making the middle of the week ideal for reviewing your budget, organizing your finances, or getting clearer about what your work is worth. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, bringing a more social and communicative energy into your weekend. You may feel inspired to reconnect with siblings, catch up with friends, or explore your neighborhood. With Venus retrograde in Libra, an old conversation or  connection could resurface, but you don’t have to respond to every message just because someone remembers your number. Choose the exchanges that actually leave you feeling good.

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Virgo, your mind may have approximately 37 tabs open as November begins, and the Last Quarter Moon in Leo wants you to close a few. This lunation activates your spirituality, solitude, and subconscious realm, encouraging you to release mental clutter and emotional baggage that’s been quietly draining your energy. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought a breakthrough involving travel, education, or your bigger vision for the future, and now you need some space to process what that means. You may feel more introspective, sensitive, or aware of old fears that tend to surface whenever you’re preparing for a new chapter. Give yourself permission to unplug and let your imagination wander without needing to turn every thought into a plan. 

Then on November 3rd, the moon enters your sign, and you may feel your motivation returning almost overnight. This is your opportunity to prioritize your personal needs, refresh your appearance, or tackle something you’ve been putting off. By the 5th, the Libra Moon shifts your focus toward money and self-worth, making the weekend a good time to review your spending and enjoy a few affordable pleasures. With Venus retrograde in Libra, you may be reconsidering what you value and whether certain purchases are actually worth it. Treat yourself if you feel inspired, Virgo, but remember that a little financial breathing room can be its own form of luxury.

Libra Sun & Rising:

Libra, how much longer are you going to let other people’s expectations dictate your  dreams? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st activates your friendship,  community, and future-goals zone, encouraging you to reconsider which connections and ambitions still feel aligned with who you’re becoming. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought revelations about intimacy, trust, or shared finances, and now  you’re seeing how those realizations affect the people you want in your corner. Perhaps you’ve been staying loyal to a social circle you’ve outgrown, or putting a personal dream on hold because nobody else seems to understand it. Leo energy encourages you to take pride in your individuality and trust that the right people will appreciate your vision, even if they don’t fully understand it yet. 

On November 3rd, the moon enters Virgo, activating your solitude and spirituality realm. You may crave more privacy, rest, or time away from the group chat to process everything that’s been happening lately. Then, on the 5th, the moon enters your sign,  bringing a welcome boost of confidence, charm, and emotional clarity. With your ruling  planet Venus still retrograde in Libra, you may feel inspired to revisit your personal style, reconnect with an old passion, or simply spend more time doing things that make you feel beautiful and appreciated. Plan something enjoyable for yourself this weekend, Libra. Your happiness deserves some attention, too.

Scorpio Sun & Rising:

Scorpio, your birthday season is officially underway, but are you still chasing a version of success that you’ve already outgrown? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st illuminates your career and public-image zone, encouraging you to release professional pressures or expectations that no longer reflect your priorities. Perhaps you’ve been trying to prove yourself to someone whose approval no longer matters, or you’re realizing that a certain career path has lost its appeal. With the sun in your sign, you have every reason to feel excited about your next chapter. Let this lunation help  you clear space for the opportunities that genuinely deserve your energy. 

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon activates your friendship, community, and future goals realm, making the middle of the week ideal for reconnecting with supportive people or getting organized around a long-term dream. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, drawing you into a more introspective mood as it moves through your solitude and spirituality zone. With Venus retrograde here, you may find yourself revisiting  memories, old attachments, or emotions you’ve been privately processing. Give yourself permission to slow down this weekend, Scorpio. Your birthday season doesn’t have to be one nonstop celebration. Sometimes the best gift you can give yourself is a little peace, a good night’s sleep, and freedom from unnecessary drama. 

Sagittarius Sun & Rising:

Sag, your next adventure is calling, but first you may need to stop carrying around beliefs that belong to an older version of yourself. The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st activates your travel, education, spirituality, and expansion realm,  encouraging you to release limiting perspectives that have been keeping your world smaller than it needs to be. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have revealed where your work, health, or daily routines need adjusting, and now you’re seeing how those changes could create more freedom in your life. Perhaps a dream you’ve been postponing suddenly feels possible, or you’re realizing that a certain path no longer excites you. With your birthday season approaching, this is a powerful time to question what you’ve been telling yourself is realistic. You might be ready for more than you’ve been allowing yourself to imagine. 

On November 3rd, the Virgo Moon lights up your career and reputation zone, helping you channel that inspiration into practical professional moves. You may feel motivated to organize a project, follow up on an opportunity, or get serious about a goal you’d like to accomplish before your birthday. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your attention toward friendship, community, and social connections. With Venus retrograde in Libra, an old friend or former collaborator could resurface, or you may feel inspired to reconnect with people you’ve missed. Enjoy the social energy this weekend, Sag, but be selective about where you invest your time. Your next chapter deserves a circle that genuinely wants to see you thrive. 

Capricorn Sun & Rising:

Capricorn, November begins with the Last Quarter Moon in Leo asking you to loosen your grip on something you’ve been trying to control. This lunation activates your intimacy and transformation zone, bringing up questions around trust, emotional vulnerability, and financial obligations. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have revealed something important about your romantic life or creative passions, and now you’re considering what you’re willing to invest in those areas. If a financial agreement or emotional attachment has become one-sided, this is a good time to reconsider its terms. You can be deeply committed to someone without taking responsibility for everything they carry. 

On November 3rd, the Virgo Moon shifts your attention toward travel, education, and bigger-picture plans. You may feel motivated to research a destination, revisit a course you’ve been considering, or map out your next professional move. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, illuminating your career and public image. With Venus retrograde in this part of your chart, an old professional opportunity or unfinished project could resurface. Take the weekend to assess whether it still aligns with your  ambitions before committing to anything. Your definition of success may have changed considerably since you first pursued it. 

Aquarius Sun & Rising:

Aquarius, who’s meeting you halfway these days? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on  November 1st activates your partnership realm, encouraging you to release relationship expectations that have become unrealistic or exhausting. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought a turning point involving home, family, or your emotional security, and now you’re noticing how your closest relationships contribute to that sense of stability. Perhaps you’ve been accommodating someone’s needs at the expense of your own, or expecting a partner to understand feelings you haven’t clearly expressed. This lunation favors honest conversations and a willingness to let old dynamics evolve. 

By November 3rd, the Virgo Moon brings your attention to shared finances, intimacy, and practical agreements. It’s a useful time to review expenses, settle an outstanding obligation, or clarify responsibilities with someone you trust. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, activating your travel, education, and expansion zone. With Venus retrograde here, you may find yourself reconsidering a trip, reconnecting with an old mentor, or revisiting a subject that once fascinated you. Give yourself something intellectually stimulating to look forward to this weekend, Aquarius. A change of scenery or perspective could be exactly what you need. 

Pisces Sun & Rising:

Pisces, that never-ending to-do list isn’t going to complete itself, but does everything on it actually need your attention? The Last Quarter Moon in Leo on November 1st  activates your work, health, and daily-routine zone, encouraging you to eliminate habits and responsibilities that are making life unnecessarily complicated. Last week’s Taurus Full Moon may have brought clarity through an important conversation or realization, and now it’s time to apply what you’ve learned. Perhaps you’ve been saying yes to too  many requests, neglecting your own appointments, or maintaining a routine that leaves you exhausted. Leo energy encourages you to take pride in how you care for yourself, including knowing when to delegate or decline. 

On November 3rd, the Virgo Moon illuminates your partnership realm, making the middle of the week ideal for discussing expectations, dividing responsibilities, or spending quality time with someone important. Then the Libra Moon arrives on the 5th, shifting your attention toward intimacy, shared finances, and emotional trust. With Venus retrograde in this part of your chart, an unresolved money matter or relationship concern may deserve another conversation. Keep things transparent, especially when it comes to shared expenses or commitments. By the weekend, you’ll have a better sense of where cooperation is making your life easier and where clearer boundaries are needed.
